title: Sorting and Filtering Data
summary: Reorder your Orders sheet by one or more columns, and use AutoFilter to show only the rows that meet your criteria.

steps.title: Putting Your Orders in Order
steps.lede: Sorting rearranges your Orders sheet rows by the values in one or more columns — oldest first, largest first, or any combination.

blocks.text: With a week of orders in your Orders sheet, you often want them in a particular order rather than the order they were entered in — oldest first, or largest amount first.

To sort a column of numbers, select a cell in that column and, on the Data tab in the Sort & Filter group, select Sort Smallest to Largest or Sort Largest to Smallest. To sort a column of dates or times, select a cell in that column and select Sort Oldest to Newest or Sort Newest to Oldest instead.

To sort by more than one column, open the Sort dialog from Data > Sort, choose the first column in the Sort by box, then select Add Level to add another column. Entries higher in the list are sorted before entries lower in the list. Each level has its own Order setting, so different columns within the same multi-level sort can be sorted in different directions.

steps.title: Single-Column Sort and Multi-Level Sort Dialog

segments.label: Single-column sort and multi-level Sort dialog walkthrough
segments.summary: The presenter sorts a dataset's revenue column largest to smallest and its division column A to Z using the right-click Sort shortcut, then explains that Excel automatically extends the sort across all adjacent columns and recognises the header row. A brief aside shows that stray text outside the table gets pulled into the sort unless you manually select only the intended range first. The presenter then opens Custom Sort — reachable via right-click or the Home tab's Sort & Filter menu — to sort division by a hand-typed custom order (Productivity, Utility, Game). Finally, two more levels are added in the same Custom Sort dialog: region sorted A to Z, then apps sorted A to Z, demonstrating that each level has its own independent Order setting and that higher levels are applied before lower ones.

steps.title: A Two-Level Sort in Practice
steps.lede: Sorting by date first and amount second puts same-day orders in descending amount order while the days stay in ascending order.

blocks.text: Sorting your Orders sheet by order_date oldest to newest, and adding a second level that sorts amount largest to smallest as a tiebreaker, puts same-day orders in descending amount order while the days themselves stay in ascending order.

steps.title: Multi-Level Sort with Independent Directions
steps.lede: Choose the correct Sort dialog configuration for a two-level sort.

public.prompt: You open the Sort dialog (Data > Sort) and configure two levels: Level 1 sorts by order_date Oldest to Newest, and Level 2 sorts by amount Largest to Smallest. What does this sort produce?

options.text: Rows are ordered by date first (oldest at the top); among rows that share the same date, they are further ordered by amount from largest to smallest.
Rows are ordered by amount first (largest at the top); among rows with the same amount, they are further ordered by date oldest to newest.
Both columns are sorted in the same direction because the Sort dialog applies a single direction to all levels.
The sort fails because you cannot mix ascending and descending directions in the same Sort dialog.

opt_b.message: In a multi-level sort, the level higher in the list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date) is applied before Level 2 (amount), so date is the primary sort key, not amount.

opt_c.message: Each level in the Sort dialog has its own independent Order dropdown. Level 1 can be Oldest to Newest while Level 2 is Largest to Smallest — they do not have to match.

opt_d.message: The Sort dialog fully supports mixing directions across levels. Each level has its own Order setting, so ascending and descending can be combined freely.

correct.message: Correct! The level higher in the Sort dialog list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date, Oldest to Newest) is the primary sort; Level 2 (amount, Largest to Smallest) is the tiebreaker for rows sharing the same date.

incorrect.message: In the Sort dialog, the level higher in the list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date) determines the primary order; Level 2 (amount) only applies within groups of rows that share the same date. Each level has its own independent Order setting.

hints: Think of the levels as a priority list: Level 1 is the main sort, Level 2 only breaks ties.
Each level in the Sort dialog has its own Order dropdown — they are independent of each other.

steps.title: Sort the Orders Sheet
steps.lede: Sort the Orders sheet by order_date ascending, then by amount descending as a tiebreaker.

public.prompt: The Orders table has amounts in column D (D2:D21) and order dates in column G (G2:G21). To sort by amount from smallest to largest, you would select a cell in column D and choose **Sort Smallest to Largest** on the Data tab. The order with the smallest amount (1800) is in row 8 (order LG-2007). Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the amount from D8, confirming you can identify the value that would appear first after sorting.

correct.message: Correct! =D8 returns 1800 — the smallest amount in the dataset. After sorting column D from smallest to largest, this row would move to the top. For dates, you would use Sort Oldest to Newest or Sort Newest to Oldest instead.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell D8. D8 holds the amount for order LG-2007, which has the smallest amount (1800) in the dataset.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The amount column is column D; row 8 holds order LG-2007 with amount 1800.

steps.title: Showing Only the Rows You Need
steps.lede: AutoFilter hides rows that don't match your criteria — the data is still there, just not visible. Clearing the filter brings it all back.

blocks.text: Sometimes you don't want to reorder your Orders sheet, you want to see only some of it — for example, only the orders above a certain amount.

To filter a range of data, select any cell within the range, select Data > Filter, select the column header's filter arrow, choose Number Filters or Text Filters and a comparison such as Greater Than, enter the filter criteria, and select OK. AutoFilter shows the data you want and hides the rest; clearing a filter redisplays all of the data.

A range or table can be filtered by more than one column at once; filters are additive, so each additional filter further reduces the subset of data shown. Filtering your Orders sheet to amounts greater than 5000, then filtering the city column to Lagos, leaves only the Lagos orders above 5000 — both conditions apply together, not separately.

annotations.text: All 20 rows visible — no filter applied
Filter icon changed — amount > 5000 filter active
Second filter on city = Lagos — rows further reduced
Row 14 (LG-2013) — only row matching Lagos AND amount > 5000

blocks.change_summary: After filtering amount > 5000 and city = Lagos, only row 14 (LG-2013, Lagos, 6800, Pending) is visible; rows 2–13 and 15–21 are hidden, showing non-consecutive row numbers.

steps.title: AutoFilter: Hiding Rows, Stacking Filters, and Clearing

segments.label: Applying AutoFilter: turning filters on, filtering by value, adding a number filter, and clearing
segments.summary: The presenter starts with a data range that already has filter drop-down arrows in the header row, then shows how to turn AutoFilter on and off by selecting any cell inside the range and clicking Data > Filter (also noting the Ctrl+Shift+L shortcut). Filtering the salesperson column to show only 'Andrew' hides all other rows without deleting or resorting them — the row numbers confirm the rows are merely hidden. A second filter is then added on the quantity column using Number Filters > Greater Than 80, so both conditions apply at once and the visible set shrinks further. Finally, the quantity filter is cleared from its drop-down menu, restoring the salesperson-only view and returning the column's icon to its default state.

blocks.group_title: AutoFilter in action: hiding rows, stacking filters, and clearing

bridge.before: Watch how the row numbers jump when rows are hidden, and notice the filter icon change on each column header when a second filter is added on top of the first.
bridge.after: The clip uses a salesperson name and a quantity column; the text’s example uses city and order amount — same additive logic. The clip demonstrates the value-checkbox method for text and Number Filters > Greater Than for numbers; the text generalizes to Text Filters as well.

steps.title: Applying AutoFilter Criteria
steps.lede: Choose the correct steps to apply a Number Filter to a range.

public.prompt: You want to filter the Orders table to show only orders with an amount greater than 5000. Starting from a cell inside the table, what is the correct sequence of steps?

options.text: Select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the amount column header, choose Number Filters > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.
Select Data > Sort, choose the amount column, set the order to Largest to Smallest, and click OK.
Select the amount column, choose Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.
Select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the amount column header, choose Text Filters > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.

opt_b.message: Sorting reorders the rows but does not hide any rows. To show only rows meeting a condition, use Data > Filter, not Sort.

opt_c.message: Conditional Formatting highlights cells visually but does not hide rows. To show only rows where amount > 5000, use AutoFilter.

opt_d.message: Amount is a numeric column, so you should choose Number Filters, not Text Filters. Text Filters are for columns containing text values.

correct.message: Correct! Data > Filter turns on AutoFilter. Clicking the column header arrow and choosing Number Filters > Greater Than lets you enter a numeric threshold. Only rows meeting the condition are shown.

incorrect.message: To filter a range to rows meeting a condition: select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the column header, choose Number Filters (for numeric columns) or Text Filters (for text columns), select the comparison, enter the value, and click OK.

hints: Filtering hides rows that don't match — it's on the Data tab, not the Home tab.
Amount is a number, so use Number Filters, not Text Filters.

steps.title: Filter the Orders Sheet
steps.lede: Apply a filter to show only Delivered orders from Lagos, then clear the filter to restore all rows.

public.prompt: The Orders table has amounts in column D (D2:D21) and cities in column B (B2:B21). AutoFilter hides rows that do not match the filter criteria — it does not delete them. Clearing the filter restores all rows. Filters are additive: filtering by city 'Lagos' and then by amount > 3000 shows only rows where BOTH conditions are true. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the amount from the first data row (D2), confirming you can read the unfiltered data.

correct.message: Correct! =D2 returns 4500 — the amount in the first data row. AutoFilter would hide rows that don't match your criteria, but D2 would still exist in the sheet. Clearing the filter would restore all rows, including any that were hidden.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell D2. The amount column is column D; the first data row is row 2.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The amount column is column D; the first data row is row 2.

steps.title: Sorting and Filtering — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now sort by one or more columns with independent directions, and filter to show only the rows that match your criteria.

blocks.text: To sort numbers, use Sort Smallest to Largest or Largest to Smallest from the Data tab. To sort dates, use Sort Oldest to Newest or Newest to Oldest. For multi-level sorts, open Data > Sort, add levels with Add Level, and set each level's Order independently — higher levels are applied first. AutoFilter hides rows that don't match; clearing the filter redisplays all data. Filters are additive: each additional column filter further reduces the visible subset.

remediation_steps.title: Multi-Level Sort: Each Level Has Its Own Direction
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a single-level sort and a two-level sort with different directions.

blocks.text: Single-level sort: sort the Orders sheet by amount Largest to Smallest — all rows reorder by amount alone. Two-level sort: Level 1 is order_date Oldest to Newest; Level 2 is amount Largest to Smallest. The result: rows are grouped by date in ascending order, and within each date the rows are ordered by amount descending. The key point is that Level 2's direction (Largest to Smallest) is completely independent of Level 1's direction (Oldest to Newest) — you set each in its own Order dropdown.

remediation_steps.title: AutoFilter: Hide vs. Delete
remediation_steps.lede: Filtering hides rows — it never removes them. Clearing the filter brings them back.

blocks.text: After applying a Number Filter (Greater Than 5000) to the amount column of your Orders sheet, rows with amounts of 5000 or less disappear from view — but they are still in the sheet. The row numbers jump (e.g. 1, 3, 7 …) because the hidden rows are still there. Clicking Data > Filter again, or clicking Clear in the Sort & Filter group, removes the filter and all rows reappear. No data was deleted.
